content.content:
## Design guidance

Forward guidance — what @documentation applies when writing docs after a feature.

### The documentation ladder

| Rung | Layer | Drift | Owns |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Storified code | none — it IS the behavior | the story; names carry context (owned by `R3-storifying.md`, cited not restated) |
| 1 | Code comments (godoc) | low — lives beside the code, reviewed with diffs | the WHY within a tiered 1–5 prose-line budget (policy below); network edges: `See docs/<feature>.md` |
| 2 | Repo docs | medium — drifts unless networked | feature/architecture docs in the doc root; point back down via greppable symbol references (edge policy below) |
| 3 | The map | minimal — short and drift-checked (Q7) | `index.md` in the doc root: one line per doc, grouped by topic; wired into CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md |

(The rung metaphor deliberately mirrors the testing composition ladder in @testing:
lowest rung that can carry it, always.)

**Placement rule:** document each fact at the lowest rung of the documentation
ladder that can carry it; higher rungs summarize and point down, never duplicate.
Good overlap: the index says "capped-jitter retries", the feature doc explains the
cap math, the godoc states the incident — each level adds detail. Bad overlap: the
same paragraph pasted at two rungs; it *will* drift. Before writing any comment,
first ask whether a rename or extraction (`R3-storifying.md`) makes it unnecessary —
rung 0 beats rung 1.

### Comment policy (rung 1 — tiered budget)

The WHY is the default content of a doc comment, and it lives inside a hard budget:
**1–5 prose lines**, scaled to the symbol's importance. Not all symbols are born
equal — the budget forces each comment to carry only the most important facts *for
that symbol*; everything else moves up to the feature doc (rung 2), where depth is
cheap, and the `See docs/<feature>.md` edge carries the pointer. This is the
placement rule made operational at write time.

**The Comment Value Toolbox** — a comment earns its lines by delivering one or
more of these values (the growable catalog with worked examples lives in
@documentation's reference.md; this list is the normative set of kinds):

- **WHY, not WHAT** — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot carry
- **Wider context** — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it
- **Important use cases / flows** — when to reach for it
- **Boundary contract** — dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior
- **Guarantees** — thread safety, nil handling, invariants
- **Network edge** — `See docs/<feature>.md` wiring a critical point into the
  repo brain

**The three-test standard** — every comment (and every rung-2 doc, for test 3)
must pass all three; @documentation applies them at write time and its
comment-critic agent enforces them adversarially after writing:

1. **Toolbox-value test**, two-sided:
   - *Floor (delete test):* a prose line that delivers none of the toolbox values
     is trash — cut it. Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler
     ("provides validation functionality"), narrated implementation, menu sections
     filled without earning their place, **review-defense narration** — the
     writer arguing with an imagined reviewer ("bounds-checked: it never indexes
     an empty slice", "deliberately narrow — not a generalized table"); a design
     choice that needs defending is defended in the feature doc, not at the code
     line — **restated repo idiom** — a comment
     justifying a convention the repo already applies everywhere (a pointer field
     meaning "omitted vs explicit zero", the standard error-wrapping style); the
     convention is documented once at rung 2 (coding standards), never
     re-explained at each use site — and **provenance and decoder-ring
     references** — PR numbers, review items, plan/decision/test-plan IDs
     ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement tags ("REQ-SVC-01"), spec section refs
     ("spec §4"), "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what
     <old system> did". A decoder-ring token fails even when it resolves inside a
     repo doc: the reader gets the fact as plain prose and the doc through the
     one See-edge — never through a code they must look up.
     The floor's lens is the 5-year reader test: a reader five years out cares how
     the product behaves NOW, never which PR or review round produced it. History
     is rewritten as present-tense rationale ("silently picking one of the TLS
     options could apply a mode the caller did not ask for"), and an
     incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the rationale for a
     constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the
     highest-value toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget. A
     crossroads whose five lines are all boundary trivia while the architectural
     WHY is missing fails, even though each line individually "adds something".
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers
   below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
   per sentence. A comment that needs a dictionary fails even when true and
   within budget. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary where a common word exists
   ("utilize" → "use", "leverages" → "uses"), stacked clauses, academic phrasing,
   and unexplained acronyms or insider jargon ("DTO", "tristate") — in the
   comment AND in the symbol name it documents.
   The test has a second half, **self-standing**: the comment must be
   understandable BEFORE reading the code. If the reader must read the code — or
   another comment ("see X's doc comment for why") — to understand this comment,
   it has negative value. State the fact in place; forward references to other
   comments fail.

**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; these are free:

- blank `//` separator lines
- the `See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line — free ONLY as its own trailing
  line; a doc reference woven into a prose sentence is not an edge, it is clutter
  in that sentence's line count
- short inline example lines, bounded at 2–4 lines — anything bigger belongs in an
  `Example_*` testable example

**Role-based tiers** — judge the tier from the symbol's role in the code:

| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary; tiny example only if it clarifies |
| **Contract** | parsing constructor (`ParsePolicy`, `ParsePort`), self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract; dos/don'ts example (free) |
| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |

**Visibility default — unexported symbols get no comment.** The tier table
prices exported API. An unexported function, type, constant, or variable
defaults to **zero** comment lines: the name is the documentation, and a name
that needs a comment wants a rename or an extraction first
(`R3-storifying.md`). The special case is **one line carrying a very
high-value toolbox item** — a constraint or fact the code cannot carry: an
ordering requirement, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number,
the package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than
that one line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the
package doc, or the feature doc. Case file:
`../examples/private-comment-noise.md` — nine commented private helpers;
four survive as one-liners, five get nothing.

**Two bounded escape hatches:**

- **Package docs in `doc.go`**: a package that genuinely earns more (data-flow
  sketch, core-types list, design decisions all pulling their weight) moves its
  package godoc to a dedicated `doc.go`, bounded at ~20–30 lines. A package comment
  inline in a regular file stays within the standard budget.
- **Crossroads expand recommendation**: the writer never self-exceeds the 5-line
  cap. When a critical crossroads would benefit from richer inline godoc beyond the
  doc reference, write within budget and append an optional, end-of-report
  recommendation — `consider expanding <Symbol>'s godoc inline — <rationale>` —
  for a human to decide later (@documentation's report carries it).

Never fill a template for its own sake — @documentation's templates are menus to
pick from, not forms to fill, and the tier budget caps how much of a menu any one
symbol can order. The one near-constant is the network edge: keep the
`See docs/<feature>.md` reference whenever a feature doc exists.

Boundary with `R3-storifying.md`, stated precisely: block comments *inside*
function bodies are R3's (its Q3 — each is an extraction candidate, and the fix is
a function named after the comment); doc comments *on* exported symbols are this
rule's (Q4 below — they must carry why/context, not restate the identifier).

### Edge conventions

- **Code → docs** (rung 1 → rung 2): a literal relative path in the comment —
  `See docs/retry-policy.md` — always on its own trailing line, never braided
  into the summary sentence (the first sentence stays clean: "Package accounts
  registers the /accounts REST endpoints.", then the See-line). Paths to docs
  are fine; docs move rarely and Q2 verifies them mechanically.
- **Docs → code** (rung 2 → rungs 0–1): cite by **exported symbol** (`Policy`,
  `ParsePolicy`); a **package or directory path** (`retry/`) only when a location
  is genuinely needed; **file paths never, line numbers never** — they are the most
  churn-prone coordinates in the repo (`R5-vertical-slice.md`'s slice reshaping
  renames and splits files as a matter of course). A renamed exported symbol is a
  deliberate, repo-wide-grep act, and a symbol is one grep or IDE-jump from its
  file — symbols are the stable coordinates. Cite the **shortest token that greps
  uniquely**: bare symbol by default; package-qualify only when the bare name is
  ambiguous under repo-wide grep. Headers especially — a header is a landmark, not
  a coordinate dump.
- **Symbol-less artifacts** (examples/, scripts/, testdata/, configs) are cited by
  **directory**, paired with the exported symbols the artifact demonstrates when
  any exist — a bare directory link loses drift detection; the paired symbols
  restore it.
- **Test references** cite the test **package** (`the logger/ package tests`),
  optionally its suite entry point (`TestSpanLoggerAPISuite`) — never individual
  test functions. Test functions have no external callers and no deprecation
  pressure, making them the repo's least stable symbols. Name one only when the
  doc's point is that specific test's design.
- **Every docs→code edge is a literal, greppable token** — never a prose paraphrase
  of code structure. Greppable edges make drift mechanically detectable (Q2);
  paraphrases fail silently.
- **Edge density stays low**: entry points and key players only. The doc maps the
  front doors; it does not mirror the tree. ASCII trees are welcome as orientation
  devices at **package/directory granularity** — a directories-only tree is just a
  set of package-path citations; file-level leaf entries are the violation. Prune
  the leaves, keep the tree.
- **Links are one-way — write an edge only when no structure implies it.** A doc's
  parent is `index.md` in its own directory, derivable from the path alone: never
  write a child→parent backlink, and never a `related:` frontmatter key — body
  links ARE the machine-readable graph. Lateral doc→doc links go inline, with the
  relationship stated in the sentence that carries the link ("auth retries use the
  capped-jitter policy — [retry-policy.md](retry-policy.md)"). The one axis no
  structure carries is code↔docs — which is exactly why those edges are written in
  both directions and grep-verified (Q2). There is no `## Related` section:
  a relationship that cannot find a sentence in the body is not worth an edge.

### Frontmatter — the doc root as an OKF bundle (rungs 2–3)

The doc root conforms to Open Knowledge Format v0.2 (markdown bundle: one concept
per file, path = identity, links form the graph). R9 applies a **stricter profile**
on top; every key it requires is a valid OKF key, so the bundle stays consumable by
any OKF tool.

- **Content docs** carry required `type` (`feature` / `architecture` / `guide` —
  the spec's one required key) and `description` (one line — it IS the doc's
  index line). Optional: `title` (the H1 is the title; the key never replaces
  it), `generated` (OKF's provenance key: ISO 8601, last substantive update),
  `tags`, and lifecycle keys `status: draft|stable|deprecated` and `stale_after`
  — the frontmatter-native form of the ⚠️ stale flag.
- **Indexes carry no frontmatter** — OKF reserves `index.md` and keeps it bare,
  with one spec-sanctioned exception: the root index carries `okf_version: "0.2"`
  and nothing else. R9 requires that key (profile rule); any other key on any
  index is a violation.
- **Drift-check rule**: a content doc's index line IS its `description`, copied
  verbatim, prefixed ⚠️ when its lifecycle says so (`status: deprecated`, or
  `stale_after` in the past) or when a bootstrap pass classified it stale. The
  description is the single source; the conformance gate (Q7) fails when an index
  line drifts from it. Sub-index lines in the root map are authored (a bare
  sub-index has no `description` to copy) — keep them short.
- **Never emit `log.md`** — OKF reserves it for change history; this rule is
  behavior-not-history, so the file must not exist in a doc root.
- **Broken links stay violations** — internally, OKF's dangling-link tolerance
  would silence the drift alarm. The *(planned)* marker (Q2) is the one
  sanctioned form of a not-yet-written reference.
- Copy-pasteable templates (content doc, root index, conventions doc) live in
  @documentation's reference.md; only the policy lives here.

### The index (rung 3) and the root

- `index.md` lives in the doc root and MUST stay short: a concise reference guide,
  **one line per doc**, grouped by topic. It is the map, not a doc.
- Past ~300 lines it becomes a **map of maps**, and the split is directory-shaped:
  each topic becomes a subdirectory with its own bare `index.md` (OKF's
  per-directory reserved file), and the root index shrinks to one short authored
  line per sub-index. The imported root stays cheap and every doc is still two hops away
  (the root map is hop 0 — it rides in with the CLAUDE.md import). The split moves
  files, so it lands in the **same commit** as the Q2-driven rewrite of code-side
  `See docs/...` paths — a moved doc with a stale code edge is a broken network
  between commits.
- **Root wiring**: the routing block is authored ONCE, in AGENTS.md — a short
  plain block (start at the index; conventions in `<docroot>/conventions.md`) at
  the repo root and, in a monorepo, nested per sub-project (closest file wins).
  It serves every tool that reads AGENTS.md instead of CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md never
  duplicates it: it embeds AGENTS.md via `@AGENTS.md` and adds the
  `@<docroot>/index.md` import (e.g. `@docs/index.md`) so the map itself is in
  context at session start.
- **`<docroot>/conventions.md` is the self-hosting doc** (`type: guide`): the
  network's own maintenance rules — frontmatter templates, link rules, the
  never-list — written for a contributor without this plugin. It is listed FIRST
  in the index, one pointer line.

### Doc root discovery and monorepos

- Discovery order: `.ai/` → `.ainav/` → `docs/`. Use the first that exists; create
  `docs/` if none does.
- Monorepo: each sub-project (its own `go.mod` or equivalent sub-project boundary)
  gets its own doc root and index; the repo-root index links the sub-indexes.
  Mechanical discovery is keyed on `go.mod` — a sub-project in another language
  keeps its docs reachable through the root index, but is outside the gate's
  bundle checks and Q2's code↔docs verification. Everything that touches code
  (sub-project discovery, the declaration set, the code-edge grep, the
  file-path ban, the symbol shapes) is supplied per language by the gate's
  adapter block; this build carries the Go adapter.
- Nesting inside a doc root is allowed; the index (or a sub-index) covers every
  file in it.

## Comment Value Toolbox

The catalog behind R9's toolbox-value test. The normative list of kinds lives in
R9's comment policy; **this catalog is the growable half** — when a new kind of
valuable comment proves itself, add it here with a worked example. Two consumers:
the writer picks from this toolbox when composing a comment (step 3), and the
`comment-critic` cites the specific toolbox item a rewrite should deliver ("swap
narrated implementation for the boundary contract this parsing constructor
needs").

Each entry: when it earns its place, and what it looks like.

### WHY, not WHAT

Rationale, incident, or constraint the code cannot carry. The default value — when
in doubt, this is the one to reach for.

```go
// ❌ ParseAddress parses an address string.            (restates the name)
// ✅ ParseAddress rejects ports below 1024: the collector runs unprivileged.
```

### Wider context

Where this sits architecturally; what depends on it. Earns its place on crossroads
symbols — the reader landing here from a grep needs to know what they're standing
on.

```go
// ❌ Queue is a queue used by the system.               (generic filler)
// ✅ Every exporter ships through this queue — backpressure starts here.
```

### Important use cases / flows

When to reach for this symbol instead of its neighbors. Earns its place when the
choice is not obvious from the names alone.

```go
// ✅ Use Snapshot for reads during a rebalance; direct reads block until it ends.
```

### Boundary contract

Dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior. Earns its place on parsing constructors
and any API whose caller needs the contract before the first call.

```go
// ✅ Accepts "3x100ms"-style specs. Zero attempts and negative delays are rejected.
```

### Guarantees

Thread safety, nil handling, invariants — promises the signature cannot express.

```go
// ✅ Safe for concurrent use; callbacks run outside the lock.
```

### Network edge

The `See docs/<feature>.md` line wiring a critical point into the repo brain.
Near-constant: keep it whenever a feature doc exists (R9 edge policy). Free under
the budget.

```go
// ✅ See docs/retry-policy.md for the incident and the cap math.
```

### What never earns a line: provenance and decoder-ring references

The anti-toolbox. PR numbers, review items, "the previous behavior" narration,
"matching what <old system> did" — change history, not behavior. The 5-year
reader test (R9's floor): a reader five years out cares how the product behaves
NOW, never which PR or review round produced it. Rewrite history as
present-tense rationale; keep an incident/ticket reference only when it IS the
rationale for a constraint.

```go
// ❌ ...must be rejected, matching the legacy backend ("more than one TLS
//    option passed"), REST v2 (which forwarded the conflict), and the CLI's
//    own client-side mutual exclusion. Silently resolving by precedence —
//    the previous behavior — picks a TLS mode the caller didn't ask for
//    (PR #481 review item 5a).

// ✅ Passing more than one TLS option is rejected (422): silently picking
//    one of them could apply a TLS mode the caller did not ask for.
```

**Decoder-ring references** are the same failure in a different costume:
plan/decision/test-plan IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement tags
("REQ-SVC-01"), spec section refs ("spec §4"). They fail even when the token
resolves inside a repo doc — a reader without the decoder ring gets nothing.
The fact goes in the comment as plain prose; the doc gets ONE trailing
See-edge; the ID stays in the doc.

```go
// ❌ userResponse is the flat REST response shape for a user account
//    (spec §4). It deliberately has NO field for the password hash — the
//    response omission is structural (T-04-02), not a zero-value
//    coincidence ... additive to the {uid} addressing scheme (D-06/D-07).

// ✅ userResponse is the flat REST response shape for a user account.
//    It has no field for the password hash or the API token, so a response
//    can never leak them.
//    See docs/accounts-api.md.
```

### What never earns a line: restated repo idiom

A comment justifying a convention the repo already applies everywhere: a
pointer field meaning "omitted vs explicit zero", the standard error-wrapping
style, the usual table-driven test shape. Each use site inherits the
convention silently; the explanation lives once at rung 2 (coding standards).
If every site carried it, the real content would drown — and the one genuine
WHY nearby would read as more boilerplate.

```go
// ❌ // Enabled is a pointer so an omitted field is distinguishable from an
//    // explicit false.
//    Enabled *bool `json:"enabled,omitempty"`

// ✅ Enabled *bool `json:"enabled,omitempty"`
```

Test before crediting a WHY: grep the repo for the same pattern. If it appears
across packages with no comment, this comment restates an idiom — cut it.

### What never earns a line: review-defense narration

The writer arguing with an imagined reviewer: defending a design choice nobody
at the code line asked about, or promising the code is safe instead of letting
the code show it. These lines are written for the PR review round; five years
later they read as noise. A design choice that genuinely needs defending is
defended in the feature doc.

```go
// ❌ Named as a single constant — not a table: a third wire format would
//    earn its own narrow check, not a generalized alias registry.
// ❌ Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice.

// ✅ (nothing — the code shows the bounds check; the design defense moves
//    to the feature doc if it is worth keeping at all)
```

### The visibility default: private symbols get no comment

Not an anti-entry — the existence rule the whole toolbox sits under (normative
in R9). The toolbox and tier menus price comments on **exported** API. An
unexported symbol defaults to **zero** comment lines; its name is the
documentation. The special case is one line carrying a very high-value toolbox
item: an ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic
number, the package's one real policy. Case file with nine worked verdicts:
`../../examples/private-comment-noise.md`.

```go
// ❌ trimUTF8BOM strips a leading UTF-8 BOM from data, returning data
//    unchanged when no BOM is present. Used both to classify a reply's
//    byte verdict (detectReplyCodec) and, for a JSON verdict, to decode
//    it (Client.ParseResponse)...
func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte { return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM) }

// ✅ (nothing — the name says it)

// ✅ special case, one high-value line:
// A BOM's lead byte (0xEF) is above the floor, so strip it before the leading-byte check.
var utf8BOM = []byte{0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF}
```

## Godoc Menus

**These are MENUS, not forms** (normative: R9's tiered comment-budget policy —
**1–5 prose lines** scaled to the symbol's role; blank `//` lines, the See-edge, and
short inline examples of 2–4 lines are free). The menus price **exported** API
only — unexported symbols default to no comment at all (R9's visibility
default; special case: one very-high-value line). The WHY is the default
content; the tier caps how much of a menu any one symbol can order:

- **Helper** (small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor) → 0–1 line, or

5	A real 143-line file from a JSON-RPC-over-HTTP client (anonymized), written by an

95	All nine symbols are unexported, so the question is existence, not size:
96	
97	| Symbol | Before | Verdict | Why |
98	|---|---|---|---|
99	| `nonJSONLeadingByteFloor` | 5 lines | one-liner survives | the WHY of the magic number ('{' is 0x7b; msgpack maps start at 0x80) — the code cannot carry it |
100	| `msgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name and value say it; "D-04 requires" is a decoder ring; "not a table, per Pitfall 3" is review-defense narration |
101	| `utf8BOM` | 6 lines | one-liner survives | an ordering constraint: 0xEF ≥ the floor, so the BOM check must run before the leading-byte check |
102	| `trimUTF8BOM` | 6 lines | DELETE | the name is the documentation; the encoding/json quirk belongs to `replyBytesForDecode`, its only decode-side caller |
103	| `detectReplyCodec` | 7 lines | DELETE | narrated implementation ("Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice") plus cross-repo provenance |
104	| `replyBytesForDecode` | 8 lines | one-liner survives | an external library quirk: encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading byte, not whitespace |
105	| `normalizeContentType` | 4 lines | DELETE | the name says it; the caller list rots |
106	| `isMsgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name says it; decoder rings and review-defense again |

113	```go
114	package jrpchttp
115	
116	import (
117	    "bytes"
118	    "strings"
119	
120	    "example.com/rpc/jsonrpc"
121	)
122	
123	const (
124	    // JSON envelopes start with '{' (0x7b); msgpack maps start at 0x80 or above.
125	    nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
126	
127	    msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
128	)
129	
130	// A BOM's lead byte (0xEF) is above the floor, so strip it before the leading-byte check.
131	var utf8BOM = []byte{0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF}
132	
133	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
134	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
135	}
136	
137	func detectReplyCodec(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec) jsonrpc.Codec {
138	    data = trimUTF8BOM(data)
139	    if len(data) == 0 {
140	        return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
141	    }
142	    if data[0] >= nonJSONLeadingByteFloor {
143	        return nonJSON
144	    }
145	
146	    return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
147	}
148	
149	// encoding/json treats a leading BOM as an invalid byte, not whitespace, so JSON strips it.
150	func replyBytesForDecode(codec jsonrpc.Codec, rawResponse []byte) []byte {
151	    if _, isJSON := codec.(jsonrpc.JSONCodec); isJSON {
152	        return trimUTF8BOM(rawResponse)
153	    }
154	
155	    return rawResponse
156	}
157	
158	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
159	    contentType := headerContentType
160	    if idx := strings.IndexByte(contentType, ';'); idx >= 0 {
161	        contentType = contentType[:idx]
162	    }
163	
164	    return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(contentType))
165	}
166	
167	func isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType string) bool {
168	    switch normalizeContentType(headerContentType) {
169	    case string(jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack), msgpackAliasContentType:
170	        return true
171	    default:
172	        return false
173	    }
174	}
175	
176	// The body bytes always pick the decoder; a disagreeing Content-Type header is only reported, never trusted.
177	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
178	    codec := detectReplyCodec(data, nonJSON)
179	    if len(data) == 0 || nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON {
180	        return codec, false
181	    }
182	
183	    headerSaysNonJSON := normalizeContentType(
184	        headerContentType,
185	    ) == normalizeContentType(
186	        string(nonJSON.ContentType()),
187	    ) ||
188	        (isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType) && nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack)
189	    bodySaysNonJSON := codec.ContentType() != jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON
190	
191	    return codec, headerSaysNonJSON != bodySaysNonJSON
192	}
193	```

195	The knowledge that was worth keeping and did not fit a one-liner — the
196	msgpack-alias carve-out, why a JSON-only client never reports a mismatch — moves
197	to the feature doc, where the exported caller's godoc points with its See-edge.
198	The exported API (`Client.ParseResponse`, the mismatch event) is where a reader
199	meets this package; that is where the tier budgets and the See-edge live.
200	
201	## The lesson
202	
203	The tier budget caps how big a comment can be; only the visibility default
204	decides whether it should exist at all. Before this case, "Helper: 0–1 lines"
205	read as permission, and a writer in fill-the-menu mode gave every private symbol
206	its tier maximum — nine comments, each locally justified, jointly unreadable.
207	The default for unexported symbols is **zero**: the name is the documentation,
208	and a name that needs a comment wants a rename or an extraction first. The
209	special case is **one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item** — an
210	ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number, the
211	package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than that one
212	line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the package
213	doc, or the feature doc.

## R11 Findings

**Lead investigated:** `internal/jobs/scheduler.go` `dispatch()` (lines 99-109), cross-referenced against `internal/jobs/registry.go`, `internal/services/snapshot_service.go`, `internal/models/job.go`.

**Q1 — same discriminator inspected in more than one place?**
`grep -rn 'Kind ==\|switch.*Kind' --include='*.go' .` →
- `internal/jobs/scheduler.go:101` `if job.Kind == "snapshot" {`
- `internal/jobs/scheduler.go:103` `} else if job.Kind == "sync" {`
- `internal/services/snapshot_service.go:96` `if job.Kind == "snapshot" {`
- `internal/services/snapshot_service.go:100` `if job.Kind == "sync" {`
- `internal/models/job.go:17` `return j.Kind == "snapshot"`

3 independent owners of the `job.Kind` discriminator (scheduler.go, snapshot_service.go, models/job.go) → violation, ≥2 sites.

**Q3 — does a `default`/trailing `else` handle "unknown kind" away from the boundary?**
- `internal/jobs/scheduler.go:105-107`: `else { return fmt.Errorf("jobs: unknown kind %q for job %s", job.Kind, job.ID) }` — inside `dispatch()`, invoked from a pool-goroutine closure (`scheduler.go:56`), i.e. deep in the call graph, not at construction.
- `internal/services/snapshot_service.go:102-103`: `return fmt.Errorf("snapshot: unknown job kind %q", job.Kind)` — same pattern, second owner of the "unknown kind" error path.
- No `ParseJobKind`/boundary constructor exists anywhere: `job.Kind` is a bare exported `string` field (`internal/models/job.go:7`, constants in `internal/models/job_kind.go:4-5`) with no validating constructor — confirmed by `grep -rn 'func.*Job\b' internal/models/` returning only `IsSnapshot`. The "maybe-unknown kind" concept is unrepresented at construction and re-litigated at every call site.

**registry.go cross-check (Q on strategy map correctness):** `internal/jobs/registry.go:13,20-21` already builds `handlers = map[string]func(models.Job) error{...}` keyed by `models.JobKindSnapshot`/`JobKindSync` — this is the right-shaped Strategy Map (single-function variance per the rule's "Interface vs strategy map" guidance). `scheduler.go`'s if-chain (`101-107`) doesn't use the map's own completeness — it re-derives the same two-way branch with a manual `else` error, duplicating the map's keyspace instead of doing a `handlers[job.Kind]` comma-ok lookup. That if-chain is the redundant, unowned copy the rule targets.

## R1 — Primitive Obsession: findings

**Lead disposition first** — `main.go:98 port == ""` and `env.go:46 v == ""` (inside `intEnv`) were checked and are NOT findings: `port` has no validation beyond a default, one call site, no domain type exists to converge on anywhere in the repo (`grep -rn "type Port\|ParsePort" --include='*.go' .` → no hits outside `net.JoinHostPort` usage) — scorecard ≈0, LOW priority, correctly left as a primitive. `intEnv`'s `v == ""` is a generic shared parsing helper already serving as the fix pattern (one owner, reused across `NUM_WORKERS`/`BATCH`/`FLAP_WINDOW_SEC`), not an inline per-call-site check.

---

**Finding 1 — Region validated/defaulted inline while a validating `models.Region` type already exists and is bypassed**

`rule | internal/env/env.go:20-24,37-42 | Q1: yes — `if region == ""` (env.go:38) defaults a raw `string` that names the domain concept "region," outside any `ParseX`/`NewX` constructor. Q2: ≥2 hits — the same "region" concept is independently defaulted/validated in `internal/services/sync_service.go:99-104` (`if region == "" { region = os.Getenv("REGION") } ... if region == "" { ... }`), and a *different* default value is hard-coded in `internal/common/constants.go:8` (`const DefaultRegion = "eu"`) versus `env.go:39` (`return "us"`) — concrete drift, the exact failure the rule's "Why" section predicts. A proper domain type already exists (`internal/models/region.go:11` `type Region string` with `ParseRegion` and `RegionEU/US/AP` constants) but `env.Configuration.Region` (env.go:15) stays a bare `string` and never routes through it. | Replace Primitive with Domain Type (route `env.Config.Region` through `models.ParseRegion`, delete the duplicate default logic) | M`

**Finding 2 — `region` in `Sync()` bypasses `models.Region`/`ParseRegion`, letting an unvalidated value into the tag**

`rule | internal/jobs/scheduler.go:121-125 | Q1: yes — `region := common.DefaultRegion; if r, ok := job.Settings["region"].(string); ok && r != "" { region = r }` performs an emptiness check on a raw string pulled out of an untyped `map[string]interface{}` field (`models.Job.Settings`), then builds `tag := "region:" + region` (line 125) with **no** validation against the known-valid set (`eu`/`us`/`ap`) that `models.ParseRegion` already enforces — an arbitrary string can reach the tag. Q2: ≥2 hits for the duplicated "region:" tag-building predicate — `internal/services/sync_service.go:106` (`want := "region:" + region`) builds the identical string independently, and the validity set {eu,us,ap} is separately re-implemented as string literals in `internal/models/tags.go:23-25` (`isRegionCode`) rather than reusing `models.RegionEU/US/AP`. Three independent owners of one rule, as the rule's "Why" predicts. | Replace Primitive with Domain Type (parse via `models.ParseRegion`, add a `Region.Tag()` method to own `"region:"+code` formatting once) | M`

**Finding 3 — `job.Kind` enum-shaped string comparisons bypass the existing named constants (and are duplicated repo-wide)**

`rule | internal/jobs/scheduler.go:101-104 | Q3: yes — `if job.Kind == "snapshot" { h = handlers["snapshot"] } else if job.Kind == "sync" { h = handlers["sync"] }` is behavior (dispatch routing) attached to a bare `string` field (`models.Job.Kind`, declared plain `string` in `internal/models/job.go:5`, no `type JobKind string`). Q1: yes — literal string comparisons are used instead of the constants that already exist for exactly this purpose: `models.JobKindSnapshot`/`models.JobKindSync` (`internal/models/job_kind.go:4-5`), which `internal/jobs/registry.go:20-21` correctly uses as map keys — `dispatch()` in the same package does not. Q2: ≥2 more hits for the identical `job.Kind == "snapshot"` predicate — `internal/models/job.go:17` (`func (j Job) IsSnapshot() bool { return j.Kind == "snapshot" }`) and `internal/services/snapshot_service.go:96,100` (`if job.Kind == "snapshot"` / `if job.Kind == "sync"`) — the same discriminator re-implemented in at least four places with no single owner. | Name enum strings (promote `JobKind` to a real type `type JobKind string` with the existing constants, and swap `dispatch()`'s literals for `models.JobKindSnapshot`/`models.JobKindSync`) | S`

content.text:
Confirmed: the only `time.Sleep` in production scope is main.go:29 (startup jitter, single call before ctx creation and serving loop — matches the rule's explicit exemption, not a finding). The `sync.Mutex` in `Scheduler` correctly sits beside `pending`/`completed`/`failed`, and every accessor (`Enqueue`, `drain`, `record`, `Completed`, `Failed`) locks it — Q4 clean. `storeOnce sync.Once` correctly serializes the single write to `store` in `registry.go`, and it's the right primitive (Q3/Q6 clean, no ceremony — this is genuinely called from multiple worker goroutines concurrently via `dispatch()`).

Two real goroutine-lifecycle gaps found:

R10 | internal/pool/workers.go:17-20 | Q2 (can the spawner stop/wait for the goroutine?): `Start(jobs <-chan Job)` spawns `env.Config.NumWorkers` goroutines (`go worker(jobs)`) and returns `void` — no `Wait`/`Close`/done-channel is handed back. Exit is provable only via the caller's implicit promise to eventually `close(jobs)` (verified: `internal/jobs/scheduler.go:47` `defer close(ch)`), but nothing lets any caller block until the worker goroutines have actually drained and returned — `Scheduler.wg` (scheduler.go:53/55) only tracks each dispatched `Job.Run()` closure finishing, not the worker's `for j := range jobs` loop actually exiting. A caller cannot know the pool has fully shut down. | Make the Goroutine Joinable (return a `*Pool` with `Wait()`, or an `errgroup.Group`/`sync.WaitGroup` held by `Start`'s caller) | M

R10 | cmd/svc/main.go:55 | Q2 (fire-and-forget in library/main code, no join at shutdown): `go scheduler.Run(ctx)` is started and never joined — `main` holds no `Wait()` call on the scheduler's `Run` goroutine itself (only `Scheduler.Wait()` exists, and it waits on the per-job `wg`, not on `Run` returning). The design-guidance exemption for fire-and-forget applies only to goroutines that "live as long as the process," but `Run` (jobs/scheduler.go:43-59) drains `s.pending` exactly once via `s.drain()` and returns — it does not loop, so given the current wiring (confirmed via `grep -rn 'Enqueue('` — the only call sites are in `scheduler_test.go`; production code never calls `Enqueue`) this goroutine exits almost immediately after boot, unobserved by `main`, with no way to detect that it exited or to wait for it before the process moves on to `srv.ListenAndServe()`. | Make the Goroutine Joinable (return/hold a done-channel or use `errgroup.Group` in `main`, `Go(func() error { return scheduler.Run(ctx) })` then join before/at shutdown) | S

Checked and cleared (no finding):
- `internal/jobs/scheduler.go:46` `s.queue = ch` — written once outside `s.mu`, but grepped `s.queue`/`\.queue\b` across the package (only hit is this one write); it is never read again anywhere, so it is not reachable from a second goroutine — not a Q4 violation, just a dead field (out of scope for R10).
- `internal/jobs/registry.go` `storeOnce`/`store` — `sync.Once` correctly guards the single write; reads via `GetStore()` are safe even though called concurrently from multiple worker goroutines (Q3 clean).
- `internal/jobs/registry.go` `handlers` map — written only once in `init()` before any goroutine starts, read-only afterward from worker goroutines — concurrent-safe (no concurrent writer).
- `internal/env/env.go` `Config`/`region` — `Load()`/`init()` run single-threaded before any goroutine is spawned in production; no concurrent writer found.
- `cmd/svc/main.go:29` `time.Sleep` — single call, main-adjacent startup jitter before any serving/cancellable loop; matches the rule's explicit Q5 exemption.
- `internal/pool/workers_test.go`, `internal/jobs/scheduler_test.go` — goroutines spawned only via `pool.Start`/`go scheduler.Run` already covered above; no additional `go`/`.Go(` sites in tests.

R10: 2 finding(s)

### Juiciness scoring

This scorecard lives here and only here — other rules and skills cite it, never
restate it.

**Behavioral (rich behavior):**
- Complex validation (regex, ranges, business rules): +3
- Multiple meaningful methods (≥2): +2
- State transitions/transformations: +2
- Format conversions: +1

**Structural (organizing complexity):**
- Parsing unstructured data into fields: +3
- Grouping related data that travels together: +2
- Making implicit structure explicit: +2
- Replacing `map[string]interface{}`: +2

**Usage (simplifies code):**
- Used in 5+ places: +2
- Used in 3-4 places: +1
- Significantly simplifies calling code: +1
- Makes tests cleaner: +1

**Verdict:**
- Score ≥4: HIGH priority — clear win, create the type.
- Score 2-3: MEDIUM priority — judgment call, present to the user.
- Score 0-1: LOW priority — do not create the type; that is over-engineering.

### The over-abstraction trap

The failure mode symmetric to primitive obsession is wrapping a primitive that has
nothing to own: no validation, no invariant, one method that merely unwraps. The
honest test: is `x.Field.IsSet()` *significantly* clearer than a well-named field or
accessor? If the real need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic,
private fields with accessors beat a wrapper type. Deep worked case — the tried
extraction, the rejection rationale, and the cheaper alternatives:
`../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.

### Placement

A juicy type must also land in the right package — feature-scoped versus
domain-generic. That decision is `R4-helper-placement.md`; the canonical example's
Stage 2 shows it applied.

## Fix pattern
No queued notifications.

1	# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper
2	
3	Demonstrates: R1
4	
5	A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
6	cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap: what a
7	correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.
8	
9	## The setting
10	
11	During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
12	lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
13	two booleans tracked related state:
14	
15	```go
16	var (
17	    isClusterCIDRSet bool
18	    isServerCIDRSet  bool
19	)
20	// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
21	if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
22	    return // both set, nothing to do
23	}
24	```
25	
26	Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
27	travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
28	step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.
29	
30	## The extraction that was tried
31	
32	```go
33	// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
34	type CIDRPresence bool
35	
36	const (
37	    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
38	)
39	
40	func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
41	    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
42	}
43	
44	type CIDRConfig struct {
45	    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
46	    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
47	}
48	
49	func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
50	    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
51	}
52	```
53	
54	## Why it was rejected
55	
56	1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
57	2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
58	3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
59	   unrepresentable.
60	4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
61	   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
62	   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
63	5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
64	   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
65	6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.
66	
67	The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
68	mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
69	type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
70	need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.
71	
72	## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming
73	
74	When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:
75	
76	```go
77	type CIDRConfig struct {
78	    ClusterCIDRSet bool
79	    ServiceCIDRSet bool
80	}
81	```
82	
83	`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
84	zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
85	surface; short-lived value).
86	
87	## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)
88	
89	When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
90	with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:
91	
92	```go
93	// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
94	// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
95	type CIDRConfig struct {
96	    clusterCIDRSet bool
97	    serviceCIDRSet bool
98	}
99	
100	func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
101	func (c CIDRConfig) ServiceCIDRSet() bool { return c.serviceCIDRSet }
102	
103	func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
104	    return c.clusterCIDRSet && c.serviceCIDRSet
105	}
106	```
107	
108	Why this beat the wrapper:
109	
110	- **Same safety** — the compiler enforces that only the parser (in the same package)
111	  can set the values; external code gets read-only access.
112	- **4 fewer lines** than the `CIDRPresence` approach.
113	- **Same readability** — `ClusterCIDRSet()` is just as clear as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`.
114	- **No wrapper ceremony** — the fields are what they are: bools.
115	
116	## The decision, tabulated
117	
118	| Approach | Types | Readability | Safety | Ceremony | Verdict |
119	|----------|-------|-------------|--------|----------|---------|
120	| `CIDRPresence` wrapper | 6 | Good | Low | High | ❌ Over-abstraction |
121	| Public bool fields (naming) | 5 | Good | Low | Low | ⚠️ Acceptable for disciplined scope |
122	| Private bools + accessors | 5 | Good | **High** | Low | ✅ Chosen |
123	
124	## The decision questions
125	
126	Before creating a wrapper type, ask:
127	
128	1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
129	2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
130	3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a
131	   wrapper.
132	4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
133	5. Does it hide complex implementation?
134	
135	Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
136	controlled. (Score it with R1's scorecard; this wrapper scores 0.)
137	
138	## The skeptic's operating rule
139	
140	**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**
141	
142	Rejecting `CIDRPresence` was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
143	that met the real need (controlled mutation) at lower cost. A bare "don't create the
144	type" would have left the original defect — uncontrolled mutation of the flags — in
145	place. The skeptic's job is therefore two moves, always together: name the need the
146	proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming when the need
147	is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled mutation, and a
148	real type (per R1) only when the need is validation or behavior.
149

1	# Anti-IF Dispatch Case: One Decision, One Owner
2	
3	Demonstrates: R11 (edges into R1, R2, R6)
4	
5	A worked study of the R11 moves on a realistic alert-notification slice: a string
6	discriminator inspected in three files becomes an interface chosen once at the
7	boundary; a single-function variance becomes a strategy map instead; and the inverse
8	case — where the skeptic kills the extraction and the switch *stays* — is worked to
9	its cheaper alternative. The compact excerpt lives in
10	`../rules/R11-conditional-dispatch.md`; this file is the full case law.
11	
12	## The disease: a decision with three owners
13	
14	The alert feature delivers over email, Slack, or PagerDuty. `Alert.Channel` is a raw
15	string (already an R1 smell), and three sites ask what it is:
16	
17	```go
18	// ❌ alert/send.go
19	func Send(a Alert) error {
20	    switch a.Channel {
21	    case "email":
22	        return smtpSend(a.Recipient, renderEmail(a))
23	    case "slack":
24	        return slackPost(a.Recipient, renderSlack(a))
25	    case "pagerduty":
26	        return pdCreateIncident(a.Recipient, a.Summary)
27	    default:
28	        return fmt.Errorf("unknown channel %q", a.Channel)
29	    }
30	}
31	
32	// ❌ alert/validate.go — drifted: pagerduty was never added here
33	func validRecipient(a Alert) bool {
34	    switch a.Channel {
35	    case "email":
36	        return strings.Contains(a.Recipient, "@")
37	    case "slack":
38	        return strings.HasPrefix(a.Recipient, "#")
39	    }
40	    return false
41	}
42	
43	// ❌ alert/retry.go — the same decision wearing an if-chain
44	func retryDelay(a Alert) time.Duration {
45	    if a.Channel == "pagerduty" {
46	        return 0
47	    }
48	    if a.Channel == "slack" {
49	        return 5 * time.Second
50	    }
51	    return time.Minute
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Why this is a defect and not a style choice:
56	
57	- **The drift already happened.** `validRecipient` returns `false` for `"pagerduty"`
58	  — not by decision, but because the second copy of the switch was not in view when
59	  the third channel landed. Duplicated discriminators drift the same way duplicated
60	  validation predicates drift (R1's Q2).
61	- **Adding SMS is a scavenger hunt.** Three known sites, plus whatever a grep misses
62	  (test helpers, a metrics label formatter). The compiler flags none of them: an
63	  if-chain has no completeness, and a switch with a `default` swallows the new case
64	  silently.
65	- **"Unknown channel" leaks everywhere.** Every switching site carries the
66	  `default:`/fall-through arm, so every function's signature and tests carry the
67	  maybe-unknown concept — the behavioral twin of R1's maybe-invalid port.
68	- **Nothing unit-tests in isolation.** Slack's recipient rule is only reachable by
69	  driving `validRecipient` with a fully built `Alert`.
70	
71	## Move 1 — Replace Duplicated Switch with Interface Dispatch
72	
73	Define the interface from the union of what the copies do: `Send` switches on
74	delivery, `validRecipient` on addressing, `retryDelay` on retry policy — three
75	methods, one type per variant:
76	
77	```go
78	// alert/channel.go
79	type Channel interface {
80	    Send(a Alert) error
81	    ValidRecipient(recipient string) bool
82	    RetryDelay() time.Duration
83	}
84	
85	// ParseChannel is the single decision point. This switch is ALLOWED —
86	// it is the one place the raw string may be inspected (R11), exactly as
87	// a ParseX constructor is the one place a raw value is validated (R2).
88	func ParseChannel(name string) (Channel, error) {
89	    switch name {
90	    case "email":
91	        return Email{}, nil
92	    case "slack":
93	        return Slack{}, nil
94	    case "pagerduty":
95	        return PagerDuty{}, nil
96	    default:
97	        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown channel %q", name)
98	    }
99	}
100	```
101	
102	```go
103	// alert/slack.go — each variant is a leaf type owning ALL its behavior
104	type Slack struct{}
105	
106	func (Slack) Send(a Alert) error           { return slackPost(a.Recipient, renderSlack(a)) }
107	func (Slack) ValidRecipient(r string) bool { return strings.HasPrefix(r, "#") }
108	func (Slack) RetryDelay() time.Duration    { return 5 * time.Second }
109	```
110	
111	`Alert` now holds a `Channel`, constructed at the boundary (the HTTP handler or
112	config loader calls `ParseChannel` and fails fast there). The three switching sites
113	collapse to method calls:
114	
115	```go
116	func Send(a Alert) error            { return a.Channel.Send(a) }
117	func validRecipient(a Alert) bool   { return a.Channel.ValidRecipient(a.Recipient) }
118	func retryDelay(a Alert) time.Duration { return a.Channel.RetryDelay() }
119	```
120	
121	(And once they are one-liners, the wrappers themselves usually dissolve into their
122	callers — the story functions call the methods directly, R3.)
123	
124	What was deleted, not relocated: every `default:` arm downstream. An `Alert` that
125	exists holds a `Channel` that exists; "unknown channel" is unrepresentable past
126	`ParseChannel`. Adding SMS is now one new file (`sms.go`) plus one `case` in
127	`ParseChannel` — no existing file changes.
128	
129	**R6 check, answered explicitly:** this interface is *earned* — it has three
130	production implementations on day one. R6 forbids interfaces whose only second
131	implementer is a test double; a dispatch interface born with one variant "for the
132	future" fails that test and should stay a switch until the second variant is real.
133	
134	### The testing payoff
135	
136	Each variant unit-tests as a leaf with literals — no `Alert` construction, no
137	switch-driving:
138	
139	```go
140	func TestSlack_ValidRecipient(t *testing.T) {
141	    assert.True(t, alert.Slack{}.ValidRecipient("#oncall"))
142	    assert.False(t, alert.Slack{}.ValidRecipient("oncall"))
143	}
144	
145	func TestParseChannel_Unknown(t *testing.T) {
146	    _, err := alert.ParseChannel("carrier-pigeon")
147	    require.Error(t, err)
148	}
149	```
150	
151	The drift bug (`pagerduty` missing from `validRecipient`) can no longer be written:
152	there is no second place to forget.
153	
154	## Move 2 — Replace If-Chain with Strategy Map
155	
156	Not every variance deserves an interface. Suppose only *rendering* varies by an
157	output format, in one behavioral dimension:
158	
159	```go
160	// ❌ before: if-chain in the middle of business logic
161	func render(a Alert, format string) string {
162	    if format == "json" {
163	        return renderJSON(a)
164	    }
165	    if format == "text" {
166	        return renderText(a)
167	    }
168	    return renderMarkdown(a) // silent default — is "yaml" markdown? nobody decided
169	}
170	```
171	
172	One behavior → a map, not three types:
173	
174	```go
175	type Format string
176	
177	const (
178	    FormatJSON     Format = "json"
179	    FormatText     Format = "text"
180	    FormatMarkdown Format = "markdown"
181	)
182	
183	var renderers = map[Format]func(Alert) string{
184	    FormatJSON:     renderJSON,
185	    FormatText:     renderText,
186	    FormatMarkdown: renderMarkdown,
187	}
188	
189	func ParseFormat(raw string) (Format, error) {
190	    if _, ok := renderers[Format(raw)]; !ok {
191	        return "", fmt.Errorf("unknown format %q", raw)
192	    }
193	    return Format(raw), nil
194	}
195	
196	func render(a Alert, f Format) string { return renderers[f](a) }
197	```
198	
199	The lookup *is* the dispatch; the comma-ok check lives once, in `ParseFormat`, at the
200	boundary. The silent markdown default — an undecided decision — became an explicit
201	error. (The map is package-level immutable data, the sanctioned shape under R8;
202	naming the enum is R1's "Name enum strings" move.)
203	
204	## Move 3 — the rejection: when the switch stays
205	
206	The skeptic's side of R11, worked honestly. The same codebase has this:
207	
208	```go
209	// alert/severity.go — the ONLY site that inspects Severity
210	func (s Severity) Color() string {
211	    switch s {
212	    case SeverityInfo:
213	        return "blue"
214	    case SeverityWarning:
215	        return "yellow"
216	    case SeverityCritical:
217	        return "red"
218	    }
219	    return ""
220	}
221	```
222	
223	A dispatch-happy reading says: three variants, extract `type Severity interface`
224	with `Info`, `Warning`, `Critical` types. Score it before moving (R1 scorecard, via
225	the over-abstraction skeptic):
226	
227	- Duplication of the discriminator: **1 site** (grep `switch .*Severity` → one hit) — +0
228	- Behavioral variance: one method, returns a constant string — trivial — +0
229	- Would the interface be earned (R6)? Three implementations, but each is an empty
230	  struct wrapping one literal — ceremony
231	
232	Verdict: **REFUTED.** The extraction would turn 12 readable lines into three files
233	and an interface for zero deletion — no duplicated switch exists to delete. The
234	cheaper alternative is R11's sanctioned form, **Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch**:
235	
236	```go
237	func (s Severity) Color() string {
238	    switch s { // exhaustive: linter fails the build when a Severity is added unhandled
239	    case SeverityInfo:
240	        return "blue"
241	    case SeverityWarning:
242	        return "yellow"
243	    case SeverityCritical:
244	        return "red"
245	    }
246	    return ""
247	}
248	```
249	
250	with `exhaustive` enabled in `.golangci.yaml`. Now the linter provides what dispatch
251	would have: adding `SeverityFatal` fails the build at this switch instead of falling
252	through to `""`. That is the whole benefit, at none of the cost.
253	
254	**The dividing line, restated:** dispatch is bought with the *deletion of duplicated
255	decisions*. Three sites collapsed to one boundary — clear win (Move 1). One
256	single-dimension variance — a map (Move 2). One site, trivial variance — the switch
257	stays, made exhaustive (Move 3). If nothing gets deleted, the abstraction is
258	ceremony.
259

1	# Switch-to-Polymorphism Case: The Ever-Growing Export Switch
2	
3	Demonstrates: R11, R6 (edges into R3)
4	
5	Adapted from production code. `../examples/anti-if-dispatch.md` works R11's canonical
6	disease — a *raw* discriminator (a kind string) inspected at three sites. This case
7	is the type-switch sibling: a value that is **already polymorphic** (an interface,
8	dispatched once at construction) gets *un-dispatched* by a type switch that unpacks
9	its fields. The decision was made when the value was built; the switch asks it again.
10	
11	Two things make this case worth its own file. First, the *obvious* refactoring
12	(extract each case body into a helper) is a trap — it shrinks the function but
13	preserves the disease. Second, the rejection axis here is different from
14	`anti-if-dispatch.md`'s Move 3: there the skeptic kills an extraction on juiciness
15	(one site, trivial variance); here the counter is **dependency direction** — a
16	situation where the dispatch move is physically unavailable and the switch is the
17	honest answer.
18	
19	## Before — the hump that grows forever
20	
21	`Patch` is an interface with one method (`Type()`) and four concrete
22	implementations, one per export destination. The converter interrogates each
23	concrete type and shovels its fields into a flat wire request:
24	
25	```go
26	func fromUpdateArg(arg UpdateArg) updateExportRequest {
27	    req := updateExportRequest{Name: arg.Name}
28	    req.Type = arg.Patch.Type().String()
29	
30	    switch p := arg.Patch.(type) {
31	    case SplunkPatch:
32	        if p.Token != nil {
33	            s := string(*p.Token)
34	            req.Token = &s
35	        }
36	    case S3Patch:
37	        req.S3Bucket = p.Bucket
38	        req.S3Key = p.Key
39	        req.S3Region = p.Region
40	        if p.Secret != nil {
41	            s := string(*p.Secret)
42	            req.S3Secret = &s
43	        }
44	    case KafkaPatch:
45	        req.KafkaTopic = p.Topic
46	        req.KafkaUseSASL = p.UseSASL
47	        req.KafkaSASLUsername = p.Username
48	        req.KafkaKeyField = p.KeyField
49	        if p.Mechanism != nil {
50	            m := p.Mechanism.String()
51	            req.KafkaSASLMechanism = &m
52	        }
53	        if p.Password != nil {
54	            s := string(*p.Password)
55	            req.KafkaSASLPassword = &s
56	        }
57	    case SyslogPatch:
58	        if p.Mode != nil {
59	            m := p.Mode.String()
60	            req.SyslogMode = &m
61	        }
62	        if p.RFC != nil {
63	            r := p.RFC.String()
64	            req.SyslogRFC = &r
65	        }
66	        if p.Facility != nil {
67	            f := p.Facility.String()
68	            req.SyslogFacility = &f
69	        }
70	    }
71	
72	    req.setTLS(arg.TLS.Expand())
73	    return req
74	}
75	```
76	
77	Three defects, and only one of them is size:
78	
79	- **The decision is asked twice (R11).** Whoever constructed `UpdateArg` already
80	  chose `KafkaPatch` — the value is an interface *because* that decision was made.
81	  The type switch re-asks it. A type switch over an interface the same package owns
82	  is always a second ask; "decide once at the edge" was violated the moment the
83	  cases appeared.
84	- **Ask-and-unpack.** The knowledge of *how a Splunk patch serializes* lives in the
85	  consumer, not on `SplunkPatch`. Each variant's wire mapping has no owner.
86	- **Silent growth failure.** Adding a `PubSubPatch` and forgetting this switch
87	  compiles clean and ships a request carrying only `Name` and `Type` — a runtime
88	  no-op with no compiler, linter, or test to catch it unless someone remembers to
89	  write one. (Mixed in, an R3 note: the business flow — identity → payload → TLS —
90	  is buried under nil-deref-convert plumbing repeated nine times.)
91	
92	## The tempting wrong fix — extract each case body
93	
94	The reflexive move is Extract Function per case:
95	
96	```go
97	case KafkaPatch:
98	    fillKafka(&req, p)
99	case SyslogPatch:
100	    fillSyslog(&req, p)
101	```
102	
103	The function gets shorter and each case reads better — and nothing real changed.
104	The switch still exists, still grows a case per destination forever, and a
105	forgotten case is still a silent no-op. This is the ceiling of function
106	extraction, not the fix.
107	
108	The falsifying question that breaks the frame: **why are we switching on type and
109	extracting data at all?** A type switch whose cases all do the same *kind* of work
110	(map my fields onto that struct) is behavior asking to live on the types. The
111	cased types already share an interface — the switch is a hand-rolled vtable.
112	
113	## After — the interface owns the behavior
114	
115	Add the fill behavior to the interface the concrete types already implement:
116	
117	```go
118	// Patch is implemented by each export-destination patch type.
119	// fillUpdate writes the destination-specific fields onto the wire request;
120	// shared fields (Name, Type, TLS) belong to the caller.
121	type Patch interface {
122	    Type() ExportType
123	    fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest)
124	}
125	```
126	
127	The orchestrator collapses to a three-beat story (R3): identity, payload, TLS.
128	
129	```go
130	func fromUpdateArg(arg UpdateArg) updateExportRequest {
131	    req := updateExportRequest{
132	        Name: arg.Name,
133	        Type: arg.Patch.Type().String(),
134	    }
135	    arg.Patch.fillUpdate(&req)
136	    req.setTLS(arg.TLS.Expand())
137	    return req
138	}
139	```
140	
141	Each destination owns its own mapping, in its own file (`splunk.go`, `s3.go`,
142	`kafka.go`, `syslog.go`):
143	
144	```go
145	func (p SplunkPatch) fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest) {
146	    req.Token = optSecret(p.Token)
147	}
148	
149	func (p S3Patch) fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest) {
150	    req.S3Bucket = p.Bucket
151	    req.S3Key = p.Key
152	    req.S3Region = p.Region
153	    req.S3Secret = optSecret(p.Secret)
154	}
155	
156	func (p KafkaPatch) fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest) {
157	    req.KafkaTopic = p.Topic
158	    req.KafkaUseSASL = p.UseSASL
159	    req.KafkaSASLUsername = p.Username
160	    req.KafkaKeyField = p.KeyField
161	    req.KafkaSASLMechanism = optStringer(p.Mechanism)
162	    req.KafkaSASLPassword = optSecret(p.Password)
163	}
164	
165	func (p SyslogPatch) fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest) {
166	    req.SyslogMode = optStringer(p.Mode)
167	    req.SyslogRFC = optStringer(p.RFC)
168	    req.SyslogFacility = optStringer(p.Facility)
169	}
170	```
171	
172	Two tiny helpers kill the repeated nil-deref-convert dance that padded every case:
173	
174	```go
175	// optStringer converts an optional enum to its optional wire-string form.
176	func optStringer[T fmt.Stringer](v *T) *string {
177	    if v == nil {
178	        return nil
179	    }
180	    s := (*v).String()
181	    return &s
182	}
183	
184	// optSecret unwraps an optional Secret for the wire request.
185	func optSecret(s *Secret) *string {
186	    if s == nil {
187	        return nil
188	    }
189	    v := string(*s)
190	    return &v
191	}
192	```
193	
194	An insert path is the same move: `fillInsert(req *insertExportRequest)` on the same
195	interface, and `fromInsertArg` becomes the same three-beat story.
196	
197	## The payoffs
198	
199	1. **Compile-time enforcement replaces a silent no-op.** A new `PubSubPatch`
200	   without `fillUpdate` no longer builds. The growth failure mode moved from
201	   "runtime request missing its payload" to "compiler error at the moment of
202	   authorship" — the strongest possible catch point. (This is R11's exhaustiveness
203	   payoff without the `exhaustive` linter: interface satisfaction *is* the
204	   completeness proof.)
205	2. **Adding a destination is a new file, not an edit.** `fromUpdateArg` is frozen
206	   at three beats; the switch version grows a hump per destination forever.
207	3. **The story survives (R3).** The orchestrator states *what* happens; each
208	   destination's *how* lives one level down, on the type that owns the data.
209	4. **The interface is earned, and sealed.** Four production implementations — this
210	   passes R6's earned-interface test (contrast: an interface whose only second
211	   implementer is a test double). The unexported method is a bonus: no code outside
212	   the package can implement `Patch`, so the implementation set is closed and the
213	   compiler-enforcement guarantee in payoff 1 cannot be bypassed.
214	
215	## Fill, don't construct
216	
217	Note the method signature: `fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest)`, not
218	`ToUpdateRequest() updateExportRequest`. The request carries fields the patch does
219	not own — `Name`, `Type`, TLS come from the surrounding argument. A constructor
220	method would either return a partial request the caller must merge (field-by-field
221	merging re-creates the original mess) or need the rest of the argument passed in
222	(the patch learns about its container). Filling keeps ownership honest: the caller
223	owns the shared fields, each patch owns its own.
224	
225	## The boundary counter — when the switch must stay
226	
227	This move has one precondition: **the package that owns the case types must also
228	legitimately own the output format.** Here both `Patch` and `updateExportRequest`
229	live in one package (a client whose API surface and wire format are the same
230	concern), so the method is natural.
231	
232	When the patch types live in a shared API package and the wire request is one
233	consumer's private detail, the move is unavailable and wrong:
234	
235	- Physically: an interface method cannot reference another package's unexported
236	  type, and exporting the wire type just to enable the method inverts the
237	  dependency.
238	- Architecturally: with multiple consumers (CLI, gateway, store), per-consumer
239	  `fill<X>Request` methods accrete every consumer's serialization onto the domain
240	  types — interface pollution from the opposite direction.
241	
242	In that situation the type switch at the consumer's boundary is idiomatic Go — the
243	honest tax of keeping the domain package transport-ignorant, and precisely the
244	boundary-adapter exemption in R11's falsifying questions. Then, and only then, the
245	"tempting wrong fix" above becomes the right ceiling: shrink the switch to pure
246	dispatch (one `fillKafka(&req, p)`-style converter per case, zero inline
247	field-fiddling) and stop.
248	
249	Note this rejection is orthogonal to the juiciness rejection in
250	`anti-if-dispatch.md` Move 3: there the extraction *could* be written but isn't
251	worth it; here it *cannot* be written where it belongs, at any price.
252	
253	The decision test, two questions in order:
254	
255	1. *Why am I switching on type and unpacking fields?* → the behavior wants to live
256	   on the types (R11).
257	2. *Does the types' package own this output format?* → yes: interface method, the
258	   switch dies. No: thin dispatch switch, and the boundary earns its keep.
259

1	// Command svc runs the device fleet backend.
2	package main
3	
4	import (
5		"context"
6		"flag"
7		"log"
8		"math/rand/v2"
9		"net/http"
10		"os"
11		"time"
12	
13		"example.com/go-mini/internal/env"
14		"example.com/go-mini/internal/handlers"
15		"example.com/go-mini/internal/jobs"
16		"example.com/go-mini/internal/repository"
17		"example.com/go-mini/internal/services"
18	)
19	
20	func main() {
21		dryRun := flag.Bool("dry-run", false, "keep devices in memory instead of the JSON store")
22		storePath := flag.String("store", defaultStorePath(), "path of the JSON device store (default from STORE_PATH)")
23		flag.Parse()
24	
25		env.Load()
26	
27		// Instances restarted by the same deploy would otherwise all hit the
28		// queue in the same instant; a little jitter spreads them out.
29		time.Sleep(time.Duration(rand.IntN(20)) * time.Millisecond)
30	
31		var (
32			store repository.Store
33			repo  repository.DeviceRepository
34		)
35		if *dryRun {
36			mem := repository.NewMemStore()
37			store, repo = mem, mem
38		} else {
39			fileRepo := mustOpenFileRepo(*storePath)
40			store, repo = fileRepo, fileRepo
41		}
42	
43		ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
44		defer cancel()
45	
46		if _, err := store.List(ctx); err != nil {
47			log.Fatalf("store not readable: %v", err)
48		}
49	
50		notifier := services.NewNotifier(os.Getenv("WEBHOOK_URL"))
51		audit := services.NewAuditLog(os.Stderr)
52		svc := services.NewDeviceService(repo, notifier, audit)
53	
54		scheduler := jobs.NewScheduler()
55		go scheduler.Run(ctx)
56	
57		mux := http.NewServeMux()
58		routes(mux, store)
59		handlers.Routes(mux, store, svc)
60	
61		addr := listenAddr()
62		log.Printf("svc listening on %s (region %s, %d workers)", addr, env.Config.Region, env.Config.NumWorkers)
63		srv := &http.Server{
64			Addr:              addr,
65			Handler:           mux,
66			ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
67		}
68		if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); err != nil {
69			log.Fatal(err)
70		}
71	}
72	
73	func mustOpenFileRepo(path string) *repository.FileRepo {
74		fileRepo, err := repository.NewFileRepo(path)
75		if err != nil {
76			log.Fatalf("open store: %v", err)
77		}
78		return fileRepo
79	}
80	
81	func routes(mux *http.ServeMux, store repository.Store) {
82		mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", healthz(store))
83	}
84	
85	func healthz(store repository.Store) http.HandlerFunc {
86		return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
87			if _, err := store.List(r.Context()); err != nil {
88				http.Error(w, "store unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
89				return
90			}
91			w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
92			_, _ = w.Write([]byte("ok\n"))
93		}
94	}
95	
96	func listenAddr() string {
97		port := os.Getenv("PORT")
98		if port == "" {
99			port = "8080"
100		}
101		return ":" + port
102	}
103	
104	func defaultStorePath() string {
105		if p := os.Getenv("STORE_PATH"); p != "" {
106			return p
107		}
108		return "devices.json"
109	}

content.text:
# Over-Abstraction Skeptic — Verdicts

I read the actual source (`internal/env/env.go`, `internal/models/region.go`, `internal/common/constants.go`, `internal/models/tags.go`, `internal/models/job.go`, `internal/models/job_kind.go`, `internal/jobs/registry.go`, `internal/jobs/scheduler.go`, `internal/services/sync_service.go`, `internal/services/snapshot_service.go`, `cmd/svc/main.go`) and grepped every claimed usage site before scoring.

---

**Finding A — CONFIRMED (score 4: R1 scorecard — Complex validation +3 via `models.ParseRegion`'s business-rule membership check already exists and is battle-tested (`internal/models/region_test.go`), plus the type already owns a second behavior, `Zone()` (format conversion +1) → clears the ≥4 HIGH bar on the existing type alone. Verified real defect: `internal/env/env.go:39` defaults to `"us"`, `internal/common/constants.go:8` defaults to `"eu"` — two independently-maintained defaults that will silently diverge.)**

This is not a proposed *new* extraction, so the over-abstraction trap barely applies — `models.Region` already has genuine validation and a real method, is tested, and is used correctly elsewhere (`Zone()`). Note for calibration: `grep` shows `env.Config.Region` has exactly **one** read site (`cmd/svc/main.go:62`, a log line), so today's blast radius of the bypass is small — but the duplicated-default bug is real and independent of that. No refutation needed; the fix is "stop bypassing a type that already earns its keep," not "create ceremony."

---

**Finding B — CONFIRMED (score 4: Complex validation +3 (reuse of `ParseRegion`), Usage 3-4 places +1 — verified `"region:"+region` string-building duplicated at `internal/jobs/scheduler.go:125` and `internal/services/sync_service.go:106` (identical pattern), and the valid-code set re-hardcoded independently in `internal/models/tags.go:23-25` (`isRegionCode`) instead of referencing `RegionEU/US/AP`.)**

Verified the sharper defect the finding undersells: `jobs.Sync()` (`scheduler.go:112-134`) appends the built tag directly (`d.Tags = append(d.Tags, tag)`) with **no call to `models.NormalizeTags`** — so an arbitrary `job.Settings["region"]` value reaches persisted tags completely unfiltered. This is a live correctness gap, not a hypothetical.
On the proposed `Region.Tag()` method: unlike the CIDR case's `IsSet()`, this isn't a bare unwrap — it ties formatting to an already-*validated* value (you can't get a `Tag()` call without going through `ParseRegion` first), which is exactly the "controlled invariant" the over-abstraction trap payload asks for. Keep it a thin one-liner (`return "region:" + string(r)`) — don't let it grow beyond that.

---

**Finding C — REFUTED (score 1: only "Used in 5+ places" +2 applies from a full re-read of the scorecard, and even that is generous; no validation is proposed (no `ParseJobKind`), no ≥2 meaningful methods, no state transition, no format conversion. Bias toward REFUTED on this marginal score.)**

The finding bundles two different fixes and only one earns its cost. Verified: `models.JobKindSnapshot`/`JobKindSync` (`internal/models/job_kind.go:4-5`) are **already declared as named constants** — untyped, but already usable as-is (`registry.go:20-21` proves it, comparing/indexing fine against a plain `string` field). `scheduler.go:101,103` using the raw literals `"snapshot"`/`"sync"` instead of those constants is a real, verified, zero-cost fix — but it requires **no new type**, only a reference swap.
The bundled ask — `type JobKind string` — is the over-abstraction trap signature: no smart constructor, so an invalid `JobKind("bogus")` remains just as representable as an invalid bare string is today; nothing becomes unrepresentable; `IsSnapshot()` doesn't move or change; no new method is proposed. This is ceremony riding on the coattails of a legitimate fix. Per Sandi Metz, the duplication here (literal vs. constant) is far cheaper to fix directly than to fix by first minting a wrapper type.
**Cheaper alternative:** swap `scheduler.go:101,103`'s literals for the already-existing `models.JobKindSnapshot`/`models.JobKindSync` constants, and swap `models/job.go:17`'s `j.Kind == "snapshot"` for the same constant. Stop there — promote to a real `JobKind` type later, per YAGNI, only if/when a `ParseJobKind` validation or a second meaningful method is actually needed.

---

**Finding D — CONFIRMED (R11 Move 2 template, verified exactly: `dispatch()` re-derives the same `handlers` map keyspace that `registry.go:20-21` already populates via `init()`, using string literals to select which literal-keyed map entry to pull, then calling it — a hand-rolled, duplicated re-statement of a lookup the map already performs.)**

Read `scheduler.go:99-109` directly:
```go
if job.Kind == "snapshot" { h = handlers["snapshot"] } else if job.Kind == "sync" { h = handlers["sync"] } else { return fmt.Errorf(...) }
```
This is provably just `handlers[job.Kind]` wearing an if-chain (note the linter already flags it: `//nolint:nestif`). Collapsing to `h, ok := handlers[job.Kind]; if !ok { return fmt.Errorf(...) }` deletes a fully redundant branch and removes the risk of the branch and the map drifting (adding a third job kind to `registry.go` without updating `dispatch()` would silently no-op today; a comma-ok lookup can't drift). This is not new abstraction — nothing is created, only duplication deleted — so it clears the bar trivially and cheaply (Effort S in practice, not M).

---
